slides.title: A mutex protects a relationship between values
slides.eyebrow: A MUTEX PROTECTS A RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN VALUES
keyPoints: Text and revision belong to one document state
All readers follow the same lock rule
The invariant should be stated before code
slides.narration: Imagine a document with text and a revision number. A reader must not observe new text paired with the old revision. These fields form one state, so the lock policy must cover both. A mutex grants one participant at a time ownership of a protected region; it does not make a neighboring field safe simply by existing in the same class. Every relevant reader and writer must follow the policy. Start with one lock around this small document state. The invariant is that each visible revision identifies the corresponding committed text. That statement tells us which operations belong together and what a snapshot must contain.

Identify the protected state and the point where the next observer may use it.

question.prompt: Would locking only the revision increment protect the text-revision relationship?
question.answer: No. Readers could still observe a mismatched pair or access text without its required synchronization.

slides.title: A snapshot is data the caller may safely keep
slides.eyebrow: A SNAPSHOT IS DATA THE CALLER MAY SAFELY KEEP
keyPoints: Copy related fields while locked
Return the copied value after unlocking
Do not expose a mutable internal reference
slides.narration: A function that returns a reference to protected text has a hidden problem: its lock ends when the function returns, but the caller may keep using the reference while another thread changes the text. Returning a copied snapshot avoids that escape. Copy both text and revision under the same lock, then let the caller use its own pair afterward. Copying has a cost and may throw if memory allocation fails, but scope-bound lock ownership still releases the mutex on that exception path. For large immutable data, a different ownership design may be appropriate. The key is to make the caller's lifetime and access rights explicit instead of exporting a reference with an expired protection promise.

question.prompt: Why does a locked getter returning const string& remain risky after it returns?
question.answer: The reference still names internal storage after the getter releases its lock; later mutation or destruction can invalidate safe use.

slides.title: Run a document update and an owned snapshot
slides.eyebrow: RUN A DOCUMENT UPDATE AND AN OWNED SNAPSHOT
keyPoints: One mutex guards text and revision
replace swaps prepared text then advances revision
snapshot returns a copied pair
slides.narration: The document starts at revision one with draft text. replace receives the new string by value, so that storage is ready before locking. It swaps the prepared string into the document and increments the bounded demonstration revision while holding the same mutex. snapshot copies both fields under that mutex. The first saved snapshot still prints 1:draft after replacement, while the second prints 2:ready. These values show that the caller owns independent snapshots, not references to changing internal storage. This compact example demonstrates the access policy with sequential calls; the class boundary is what prevents callers from reaching the fields without the lock.

question.prompt: Why does the first snapshot still contain draft after replace?
question.answer: It owns a copied string and revision value, independent of the document’s later internal state.

slides.title: Scope-bound unlocking survives an exception
slides.eyebrow: SCOPE-BOUND UNLOCKING SURVIVES AN EXCEPTION
keyPoints: Reject the candidate before changing state
The guard releases ownership while unwinding
A later operation can acquire the same mutex
slides.narration: A lock_guard ties mutex ownership to a scope. This program locks, rejects a negative candidate by throwing, and leaves the protected value unchanged at seven. As the exception leaves the block, the guard's destructor unlocks the mutex. A later guarded operation acquires that same mutex and increments the value to eight. The output rejected=true value=8 checks both the rejection and later usability. Automatic unlocking does not itself roll back partially changed data, which is why validation happens before assignment here. If we had changed several fields before throwing, we would still need a design that restores or explicitly represents a valid failure state.

question.prompt: Does lock_guard automatically restore data that was partially changed before an exception?
question.answer: No. It releases the mutex. The operation must separately preserve or restore its state invariant.

slides.title: Where the simple approach fails
slides.eyebrow: WORKSHOP · CONTRACTS AND EVIDENCE
keyPoints: Using a separate unrelated mutex at each call site provides no shared exclusion. Protecting only one balance also fails to protect the total.
A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Give each worker its own mutex. Both can then enter their critical sections at the same time and race on the accounts.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Use the same synchronization object for every access governed by the invariant. Protect readers as well as writers if they can run concurrently.

slides.title: Mutexes
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A mutex coordinates exclusive ownership.
A thread acquires it before accessing protected mutable state and releases it afterward.
Correct use establishes both exclusion and the ordering needed to observe prior protected updates.
A mutex protects a rule about state , not a particular memory address by magic.
slides.narration:
A mutex coordinates exclusive ownership. A thread acquires it before accessing protected mutable state and releases it afterward. Correct use establishes both exclusion and the ordering needed to observe prior protected updates. A mutex protects a rule about state , not a particular memory address by magic. If another function accesses the same state without the mutex, the rule is broken. Keep the state private behind an interface where practical so that callers cannot bypass the protection accidentally.

In plain English: This is a coordination rule that helps multiple workers share information without stepping on each other's work.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: The ledger below starts with 1000 units on the left and zero on the right.

slides.narration: The ledger below starts with 1000 units on the left and zero on the right. Four workers each move 100 units, one at a time. One mutex protects both balances, and every transfer preserves their sum. Companion listing: ch47/ledger.cpp The expected output is left=600 right=400 . No transfer can observe the half-updated pair because all protected access uses the same mutex. Returning a copied snapshot keeps callers from retaining a reference that would bypass the lock after the function returns. The arithmetic is bounded by the initial total, so the example’s unsigned additions cannot exceed 1000. A general financial or inventory system would need explicit numeric range and domain rules rather than assuming those bounds remain true for arbitrary inputs.

slides.title: Keep validation inside the transaction it protects
slides.eyebrow: KEEP VALIDATION INSIDE THE TRANSACTION IT PROTECTS
keyPoints: Check funds or capacity under the same lock
A stale snapshot cannot authorize a later update
Revalidate after releasing and reacquiring
slides.narration: Suppose two requests each inspect a balance of ten and each plan to remove eight. If the funds check occurs before acquiring the mutex, both may decide that the operation is allowed. Serializing only the subtraction cannot repair the stale decisions. The check and update belong in one critical section because they establish one transaction. Expensive work can sometimes be done on a copied snapshot outside the lock, but applying its result may require checking a version or other assumptions again. Shortening a critical section is useful only when it preserves the same invariant. A faster path that admits impossible state is not an optimization of the original contract.

slides.title: Lock ownership also orders memory access
slides.eyebrow: LOCK OWNERSHIP ALSO ORDERS MEMORY ACCESS
keyPoints: Unlock and later successful lock connect protected operations
One lock policy includes readers
A separate reader lock can break the agreement
slides.narration: Mutual exclusion keeps protected operations from overlapping, and the mutex relationship also orders visibility of earlier protected updates to the next owner. That is why a reader must use the same policy as a writer even when it never changes data. A second unrelated mutex in the reader does not coordinate with the writer's mutex. The code may contain two locks and still contain a data race. Keep the ownership rule close to the data definition and expose operations that enforce it. In the document example, both replace and snapshot use mutex_, making the relationship visible instead of relying on each caller to remember a comment.

question.prompt: Why does giving readers their own unrelated mutex fail to coordinate with writers?
question.answer: The locks exclude only their own owners; there is no shared exclusion or ordering relationship between the separate mutexes.

slides.title: Choose lock_guard or unique_lock for the actual job
slides.eyebrow: CHOOSE LOCK_GUARD OR UNIQUE_LOCK FOR THE ACTUAL JOB
keyPoints: lock_guard fits one uninterrupted ownership scope
unique_lock supports controlled release and waiting
Both express ownership more clearly than manual pairs
slides.narration: A lock_guard acquires a mutex and releases it at the end of its scope. It is a good fit when an operation should remain protected throughout one block. A unique_lock keeps ownership state that can be released and reacquired, which condition-variable waiting needs. That extra flexibility also creates more states to reason about. Do not use manual lock and unlock calls merely to avoid a small owner object; an early return or exception can skip the unlock. Choose the simplest owner that supports the operation. Then ensure that object destruction occurs after the invariant is restored and before any long wait that depends on another thread using the same mutex.

slides.title: Coarse and fine locks trade different costs
slides.eyebrow: COARSE AND FINE LOCKS TRADE DIFFERENT COSTS
keyPoints: One lock simplifies a shared invariant
More locks may permit independent work
Cross-region operations need an acquisition policy
slides.narration: A single mutex around a small document or ledger is often the clearest starting point. It makes the state invariant easy to inspect and avoids many ordering problems. If measurements later show that unrelated operations wait behind it, separate locks may help. But an operation spanning those regions now needs coordinated acquisition and a proof that no cycle can form. More locks also cost memory and can increase cache traffic. The right comparison is a measured workload with the same semantics, not the number of mutexes in a diagram. Keep the coarse version as a correctness reference while experimenting with finer protection.

slides.title: Review what escapes while the lock is held
slides.eyebrow: REVIEW WHAT ESCAPES WHILE THE LOCK IS HELD
keyPoints: Unknown callbacks may reenter or acquire other locks
References can outlive protection
Exceptions can expose incomplete state
slides.narration: Inspect the exits from a critical section, not just its entrance. A callback may run arbitrary code, reenter the same component, or acquire another lock in an unexpected order. A returned reference may let someone access state after protection ends. An exception may release the mutex while the fields no longer satisfy their relationship. Each escape needs a policy. Often the operation can commit a small consistent update, copy a notification value, unlock, and then invoke outside code. That does not make every callback safe automatically; the callback observes a completed event rather than participating inside the protected transaction.

question.prompt: What should hold when a guard releases its mutex during exception unwinding?
question.answer: The protected state must still satisfy its documented invariant or an explicitly documented valid failure state.

slides.title: Test conservation and consistency, not only completion
slides.eyebrow: TEST CONSERVATION AND CONSISTENCY, NOT ONLY COMPLETION
keyPoints: Check related-field snapshots
Exercise rejected operations and exceptions
Measure contention only after correctness
slides.narration: A concurrency test that merely waits for workers to finish can miss lost items, mismatched versions, or duplicated transfers. Test the rule that the mutex is intended to protect. For a document, verify that each snapshot's revision matches its text. For a ledger, verify the conserved total and the exact number of successful bounded transfers. Add rejected inputs and exceptions so later normal operations prove the mutex and state remain usable. Then measure contention if the feature needs more throughput. Keeping tests tied to invariants makes maintenance safer because a future optimization must preserve a concrete behavior rather than a vague claim that the class is thread-safe.

example.title: Protect a whole invariant
explain: Constructing lock_guard locks guard. Its destructor unlocks at the end of this scope, including stack unwinding.
The source balance must cover the transfer before the first update. This fixture checks ten units are available.
Debit the first balance while holding the lock. At this intermediate point the conservation rule is temporarily incomplete.
Credit the second balance before releasing the same lock. Other participating operations must use this lock too.
The assertion checks the restored total of 100 while the protected state is still locked. Locking each update separately would expose an invalid intermediate total.
example.invariant: Every participant must use the same mutex for the protected balances. A complete transfer restores the conserved total before releasing the lock.
